articleTitle: Voltage distortion measurements between 9 kHz and 150 kHz at ultra-rapid EV chargers in the UK
abstract: This paper presents voltage distortion measurements in the 9 kHz to 150 kHz frequency range at sites with ultra-rapid EV chargers. The voltage distortion caused by Electric Vehicle Charging Station (EVCS) chargers if left unrestrained may damage other nearby equipment installed on the network, therefore standardized measurement of distortion is crucial to prevent this harm. One of the potential candidates as a standardised measurement method was applied and the results for one of the sites briefly exceeded compatibility levels defined in IEC 61000-2-2. Tools to describe and analyse the results are given, demonstrating how some distortion frequencies are related to the current drawn by the chargers and others remain constant if any charging load is present. Once a measurement method in this frequency range is fully standardised then it is hoped that these tools can be developed into a protocol for the soon to be required power quality surveys.

articleTitle: Megawatt charging for electric trucks in a multidirectional microgrid
abstract: Decarbonisation of the road freight sector, particularly trucks or heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), is necessary to achieving net zero commitments. Electric HGVs (eHGVs) are an environmentally sustainable solution, but their economic viability is uncertain. This paper addresses the challenges of eHGVs charging infrastructure and discusses an innovative solution with high-power, megawatt charging supported by a microgrid. This technology enables the integration of local generation, and storage, therefore minimising reliance upon the electricity distribution network, and supporting high-power, megawatt charging infrastructure. The energy management and economic opportunities offered by smart charging (V1G) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operation in a microgrid may reduce the total cost of ownership (TCO). The proposed microgrid incorporates power components including high-power, megawatt chargers, battery energy storage system (BESS), flywheel energy storage system (FESS), potential photovoltaic generation, along with legacy electricity distribution network connection and other consumer loads at site. A computer simulation model was developed to support feasibility assessment, microgrid design, and component sizing for any site location. Use of this simulation model will assist fleet operators to make informed decisions about eHGV charging infrastructure investment.

articleTitle: Usage analysis of public AC chargers in the UK
abstract: In the United Kingdom, approximately 56% of the total charging network, consisting of forty thousand charge points, is comprised of fast AC chargers. However, there exists a significant lack of information regarding usage patterns, which poses a challenge for making informed decisions about future infrastructure planning. This paper focuses on a statistical analysis of the usage patterns of 416 public AC chargers (7 kW) in the UK, based on a dataset comprising over ten thousand charging sessions. The data was collected from one of the UK's largest AC charging network operators over a four-month period (April to July 2022). The study specifically examines the charging demand (measured in kWh) and utilisation rates of chargers located in four different types of parking lots: multi-storey, workplace, on-street, and surface car parks. The analysis reveals that the median charging demand remains consistent across different locations, but there is a high standard deviation in locations with parking restrictions. Two different utilisation metrics, namely sojourn-based and energy-based, are employed to assess the utilisation rates. The results indicate that the overall median utilization rates are generally low, with most locations recording rates below 5%. These findings contribute valuable insights for effective planning and optimal allocation of investments aimed at expanding charging infrastructure.

articleTitle: Efficient electric vehicle charging infrastructure planning using data-driven optimization
abstract: This paper presents a high-level overview of a data-driven methodology for optimising the implementation of policy commitments in the transportation sector, specifically focusing on electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure in Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom. The study utilises a simulation model provided by the industrial partner, Arup Group Limited, and combines it with a genetic optimization algorithm inspired by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and fuzzy logic. Four future energy scenarios from National Grid are considered to predict EV quantities and the energy demand, reflecting varying levels of decarbonisation and societal change. The optimization algorithm is applied to each scenario to determine the optimal charging point types, locations, quantities, total capital and operational expenditures, and operating hours of the charging points. This paper provides a high-level explanation of the methodology and results, without delving into the mathematical equations or detailed aspects of the simulation and optimization processes. The proposed methodology demonstrates a promising approach to efficiently implement policy commitments in the transport sector, particularly in the context of EV charging infrastructure, enabling local authorities to effectively plan and manage the transition to zero-emission vehicles.

articleTitle: Reprocessing of retired EV batteries for secondary use: pulse test method - results
abstract: It is known that EVs have stringent performance requirements, and hence their batteries need to be removed from service when their performance is inadequate. Such retired batteries can be used in secondary applications such as energy storage systems, grid stabilization, and EV charging infrastructure. Battery sorting needs to be done for selecting suitable batteries, to ensure safety, and to determine the economic viability of secondary applications. In this paper, the use of pulse test method is described for state-of-health determination of retired EV batteries.

articleTitle: Optimising electric vehicle charging infrastructure in Dublin using GEEcharge
abstract: Range anxiety poses a hurdle to the adoption of Electric Vehicles (EVs), as drivers worry about running out of charge without timely access to a Charging Point (CP). We present novel methods for optimising the distribution of CPs, namely, EV portacharge and GEECharge. These solutions distribute CPs in Dublin, in this paper, by considering the population density and Points Of Interest (POIs) or road traffic. The object of this paper is to (1) develop and evaluate methods to distribute CPs in Dublin city; (2) optimise CP allocation; (3) visualise paths in the graph network to show the most used roads and POIs; and (4) evaluate the efficacy of the solutions. The criterion for success used in this paper is that, an EV is within a 500m range of the CP, when it runs out of charge. Our findings show that, in Dublin City, 121 CPs are an optimal number for a 1km<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> area. Discrete event simulation establishes the superiority of the GEECharge method, which exhibits a 2.2% higher efficiency compared to the EV Portacharge method. Population density, POIs, and road usage patterns are crucial factors that demand careful consideration when formulating a comprehensive framework for CP distribution.

articleTitle: Impact of temperature on EV charging and the distribution network
abstract: Widespread electric vehicle (EV) adoption is occurring as countries move to decarbonise transportation. However, EV charging can have an impact on the distribution network, as operators ensure that voltage, current and capacity limits are satisfied. Therefore, electric vehicle profiles become a key input to planning assessments. Weather can affect the driving habits of EV users, charging behaviour and charging efficiency, altering these profiles. This paper investigates the significance of temperature on EV charging profiles using at home EV charging records and local temperatures in Austin (Texas, US). At the same time, the impact of different EV charging behaviours on the distribution network is illustrated. The results argue that EV charging demand is temperature sensitive, and only using average EV charging profiles could significantly underestimate peak demand. Therefore, network planning should account for temperature variations when determining electric vehicle hosting capacity and charging infrastructure needs.

articleTitle: Reprocessing of retired EV batteries for secondary use: pulse test method - various challenges and observations
abstract: It is known that the pulse test on a battery for finding its internal resistance enables fast and accurate battery state-of-health (SoH) determination. This paper details the pulse testing methodology that is deployed as a part of the project for the rapid SoH assessment of the retired Electric Vehicle (EV) batteries so that their sorting and grouping can be done for second-life applications. Various preliminary challenges faced such as noise in the measurements, dissimilarity between different test system outcomes, the effect of temperature on the internal resistance, and others are discussed.

articleTitle: UK electric vehicle charging use cases for optimised infrastructure roll out
abstract: This paper presents an approach to determining the type and sizing of the electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure required to meet the charging demand of the UK vehicle parc once electrified. The findings indicate that while convenient home charging and destination charging can fulfil a portion of the UK's charging demand, public rapid charging emerges as the primary solution, satisfying approximately 65 to 75% of the total EV charging demand. Based on a 40% utilization rate, it is estimated that the deployment of 112,000 to 130,000 rapid chargers would effectively meet this demand. This ensures commercial viability and scalability of the UK EV infrastructure, but also promotes sustainability by significantly reducing the number of superfluous charging infrastructure assets, the associated grid impact, and the environmental impact on raw materials and supply chain. Whilst convenient home charging remains an important EV charging option, public EV charging infrastructure is key to deliver the national EV charging demand in a robust and sustainable way.

articleTitle: Power demand considerations at electric vehicle charging hubs
abstract: Charge profiles for a range of Battery Electric Vehicles (EV) were tested on chargers with an output power of 300kW. These charge profiles were then used in a model to show the power a charging hub might require at busy times. These results show that for a charging hub with 10 chargers there is little chance of requiring a grid connection of 3MW (10 × 300kW). There are business advantages to be exploited by understanding this information which could be used to reduce the cost of the infrastructure or to increase energy sales. The data can also be used to show how there would be little or no impact to the customer in terms of charging time if a site is power limited when load is managed correctly.

articleTitle: Connectmore: enabling connections for EV stakeholders
abstract: This paper presents the ConnectMore tool, developed by EA Technology as part of the Innovation Project, Charge [1], funded by Ofgem's Network Innovation Competition. SP Energy Networks (SPEN), partnered with EA Technology, PTV Group, and Smarter Grid Solutions (SGS) to develop a self-service tool that supported customers seeking to install new EV chargepoints on their electricity distribution network. Combining the specialist domain knowledge of the project partners, with SPEN's network data, the ConnectMore Tool enables optimised geospatial planning of EV charging point locations between now and 2050. This is achieved through combining forecast EV energy requirements with modelled grid capacity, and the cost to implement the proposed new connection. Where a flexible connection is technically viable, the tool will identify this to SPEN, potentially enabling customers to secure a flexible connection more quickly than a firm connection would otherwise require. The tool allows customers to quickly test multiple locations on the distribution network, receive an estimated cost in minutes, rather than weeks, reducing effort and costs for SPEN, and hence reducing overall costs for customers, whilst accelerating the deployment of new charging points and maximising utilisation of the available grid capacity.

articleTitle: Off-grid charging of electric aircraft facilitated by renewables coupled with energy storage
abstract: This paper presents a methodology for optimising the sizing of a flight school electric aircraft off-grid charging system powered by renewable energy sources and including energy storage to meet the Jet Zero strategy target for a greener ground-based infrastructure to achieve net zero aviation in the United Kingdom by 2050. The analysis uses solar and wind data measured at an airfield in the south east of England. Annual charging load profiles were created using the specification of a battery electric aircraft used for pilot training. The results show that continuous usage of one electric aircraft throughout the year for three training sessions per day requires an off-grid system with a minimum solar and wind capacity of 22 kW and 2.5 kW, respectively, coupled with 133 kWh battery storage. Using two electric aircrafts to allow a quick turnaround at the flying school increases the size of the system to 43 kW for solar, 5 kW for wind and a battery of 264 kWh. The payback period for both scenarios is 8.4 years, assuming the price per kWh is £0.51/kWh similar to the current rate of public fast/slow charging station and decrease to 5.5 years when the charging price is set at Rapid/Ultra-rapid station level of £0.75/kWh.

articleTitle: Optimal location of electric vehicle charging station in unbalanced power distribution system
abstract: Current environmental concerns over greenhouse gas emissions and the finite supply of fossil fuels have a direct impact on the switch from conventional to Electric Vehicles (EVs). As a result, the innovation and revolution of EV technology have accelerated, particularly in storage and charging facilities. This will increase the demand for EVs, and therefore, there will be a need for more charging facilities. However, putting EVs into use on a wide scale would present many difficulties, especially on power distribution networks. The massive and random location of EV Charging Stations (EVCS) can introduce additional power losses, affect voltage regulation, and exacerbate the voltage unbalance level. Therefore, in this research paper, unbalanced load flow calculation and optimisation techniques will be introduced to define the optimal location of EVCS that will reduce their adverse connection impact. The case studies investigate the impact of random location EVCS and then highlight the importance of determining their optimal location. The findings emphasise that optimal strategies in placing EV charging infrastructure can enable the efficient and sustainable integration of EVs into the power grid.

articleTitle: EV charge infrastructure demand forecast: a data-led approach
abstract: Electric Vehicles (EV) are quickly becoming a popular solution for car drivers looking at making the switch from Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles to a greener alternative. A significant amount of the energy demand in transportation is moving from fossil fuels to the electricity network. Arup have developed a forecasting model and methodology to determine the charging infrastructure demand associated with transitioning ICE vehicles to EV. The forecast model enables analysis of EV charge infrastructure demand and provides insight to Local Authorities and other Stakeholders under several scenarios, applying assumptions, including EV uptake, charging schemes/incentives and user behaviour. When deploying charge points, having a strategy in place maximises charge point investment benefits, Arup believes undertaking current and future demand modelling will better inform wider strategy. This paper describes the methodology used to develop several EV strategies based on a data-led approach, for local and wider Government in the British Isles.

articleTitle: From planning to deployment - insights into installing publicly-accessible journey EV charging infrastructure
abstract: Deploying publicly accessible electric vehicle charging infrastructure involves engaging with multiple stakeholders from various organisations to ensure successful project delivery. When installing a fleet of charging points across a wide area, the number of stakeholders increases often resulting in a disjointed or non-standardised experience for EV infrastructure developers. Based on real-world learnings, this paper suggests several improvements that could be implemented by distribution network operators that would help streamline infrastructure deployment and help accelerate the uptake of zero-carbon transport solutions.

articleTitle: Electric vehicle charging impacts on rural power grids
abstract: Electrification of the transport sector is well underway, with large legislative and economic pressures driving the private passenger industry transition. In 2030 we are expected to see the end of petrol and diesel vehicle sales in the UK, pushing consumers to make this switch, a transition that rural motorists will also be affected by. This UK wide uptake of Electric Vehicles (EVs) has led to concerns over the capabilities of current grid infrastructure capacity, should high adoption rates be reached. These concerns are only exacerbated in rural areas due to typically weaker infrastructure when compared to the urban counterpart. An EV Charging Model, based on a Travel Demand Model, combined with substation meter readings was used to analyse the grid impact, failure points and forecasted timelines until this large scale EV adoption scenario could become a reality.

articleTitle: Network capacity trading for managing EV charging in low-voltage networks
abstract: Significant growth in electric vehicle (EV) charging demand will place more power demand on low-voltage distribution systems than these networks were initially designed to accommodate. Without any energy management, uncontrolled load usage can cause significant issues to these networks, including exceeding limits on the maximum transformer power, maximum line currents through cables and the maximum and minimum permitted voltage at each house in the network. This paper introduces a novel approach to the management of power demand and generation in low-voltage residential networks, focusing here specifically on EV charging with solar PV generation and battery storage, through the trading of Network and Phase Capacity Tokens (NCTs and PCTs) between houses. By equating the network load capacity and each individual load and generation to a quantity of NCTs and PCTs, the proposed Capacity Token trading is shown to ensure that none of the network limits are exceeded while giving each house greater control over their energy usage and providing a more decentralised solution to network energy management.

articleTitle: Low-voltage assemblies for electric vehicle charging applications
abstract: As societies move towards carbon neutral, the electric vehicle is becoming increasingly important. Consequently, low-voltage assemblies are essential to control and protect the supplies to chargers in hubs. The electric vehicle charging application is more demanding than that of most low-voltage assemblies. In a number of instances, the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) Standards and British Standards (BS) are behind the needs of this quickly evolving application. All circuits can be fully and continuously loaded at the same time, and in some instances the assembly is managed to its rated full load current for long periods of time. Earthing and earth leakage protection are often complex and misunderstood. Protection against an open protective earth neutral (PEN) conductor can be required. When the assembly is located outdoors, as is often advantageous, solar effects combined with full load currents require particular attention. When assemblies are located in areas accessible to the public, consideration needs to be given to the risks associated with their exposure to the public and the very unlikely event of an arcing fault within the low-voltage assembly. This paper identifies the specific needs of low-voltage assemblies for electric vehicle charging installations and provides guidance to specifiers who require satisfactory performance from their low-voltage assemblies.

articleTitle: Modelling vehicle to grid demand on LV networks
abstract: Load profiles are used by Distribution Network Operators to design and model new and existing electricity networks. This article focuses on the development of profiles by EA Technology for the operation of vehicle to grid (V2G) EV charging, using data from 'Electric Nation – Powered Up', run by CrowdCharge. With these profiles it is then possible to assess the impact of V2G on existing and new LV networks using prevailing modelling approaches. In the UK, the ACE49 modelling approach is widely used for the design of LV networks. This approach assumes that demand in each half hour is normally distributed, and can be modelled probabilistically using the mean and standard deviation to design networks around (typically) 90<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">th</sup> percentile demand. Analysis of the trial data showed that V2G demand/generation is not normally distributed. The combination of more vehicles needing to be recharged each night (due to discharging in the evening) and the tariff incentive greatly reduced the diversity in charging demand. Profiles were developed by combining the expected probability of a car being connected (which was normally distributed) with the realistic per vehicle worst case demand.

articleTitle: A bidirectional EV charger with voltage based control
abstract: A device that can control power flow to and from an EV has lots of applications. There are trials already published demonstrating the efficacy of such devices, with savings available due to time of use tariffs. This is different in that it uses control signals (voltage) from the grid in real time, to determine whether the EV should be taking power from the grid or delivering it back. A section of the power network is modelled in the first step to generate a range of possible voltages which trigger G2V and V2G, respectively, at the network's last or weakest busbar. The Electric Vehicle is charged or discharged in the second step using a DC/DC Buck-Boost bilateral converter and results are available. Such a device is preferable to a time of use control as it is shown to cope with unexpected changes in the weather, or other societal changes. The control signal is individual to each charging point.

articleTitle: Comparative study of active front end converters for off board EV fast chargers
abstract: The recent fast paced evolution of electric vehicles has brought dramatic changes to the automobile industry. Car manufacturers have been hastily switching their development from combustion engine to electrical drive. Fast off board chargers are emerging in every public place. This paper presents an industrially focused comparison of AC/DC converters. The volume and cost of each topology along with its filter is estimated to better understand the impact of the differences between them.

articleTitle: Optimal sizing of stand-alone energy systems incorporating battery capacity fading
abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are one of the key elements for designing a stand-alone system based on renewable energy generation. The capacity of these equipment, however, starts to fade due to charge cycling and ageing. In this paper, a planning scheme is presented for supplying electric vehicle (EV) charging stations by a stand-alone system composed of wind and PV generation, and batteries. The approach is based on a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulation and a binary expansion method is utilized to tackle the nonlinearities of the problem. After quantifying the degradation behaviour of the battery by solving the optimization problem, its capacity is modified to be able to charge and discharge according to the output of the sizing program. The formulation is applied to a LiFePO4 (LFP) battery technology, and the results illustrate how the battery degradation is able to impact the final capacity and planning costs for the system. For a reliability level of 99%, a 139.78kWh with a total degradation of 18.74kWh is calculated. Also, for the reliability level of 90%, the calculated capacity and total degradation are 207.23kWh and 40.86kWh respectively.

articleTitle: An inspection and testing platform solution for electric vehicle supply equipment to comply with the electricity at work regulations 1989
abstract: The United Kingdom has committed to becoming a Net Zero country by 2050 and a major part of the proposals are the electrification of vehicles. Electric vehicle charging will need to be installed and maintained to a safe standard for the target to be met. A targeted literature review carried out shows the need for a robust inspection and test regime to help electrical duty holders comply with the current statutory regulations. Research methods such as structured interviews, questionnaires and sample site inspection and tests were utilised to achieve the project aims. The experiments and analysis identified that many duty holders do not have a regime of inspection and testing in place. This resulted in many supply units not complying with the statutory regulations and therefore posing a safety risk to the end user. A link between the number of reported deviations from the current standards increased with the age of the installed equipment. The current available testing equipment was used in real world scenarios and analysis completed to make sure the correct, robust, and accurate instrument was chosen. The report has concluded an inspection and test methodology and reporting standard does not exist. The condition of the installed UK charging network is not in the best condition with a significant number of units out of service at any one point. To improve the current installed charging network, and to maintain all future units, the designed inspection and test methodology and reporting standard included in this report could be utilised.

articleTitle: Control & modelling of wireless charging system for electric vehicles and their application in dynamic scenarios
abstract: Dynamic Wireless Charging (DWC) for Electric Vehicles (EVs) offer a high level of convenience and autonomy alongside potential cost savings on battery size and charging infrastructure. To achieve efficient wireless charging, various control strategies have been proposed, while the control for dynamic charging is still under development. This paper presents an efficient dualsided control strategy without the need for communication between the primary and secondary sides. Linear controllers are used to control system parameters voltages and output characteristics. The control methodology is demonstrated with a 4.3kW simulation, achieving 93% steady state efficiency. Finally the control shown steady output control with dynamic application, successfully control system variations.

articleTitle: Designing EV charging stations deployment through holistic simulations: the SANEVEC project
abstract: To determine the optimal location of the large number of urban public charging stations that will have to be deployed in the following years to transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is a challenging task, as it is intimately interconnected with the complexity of urban traffic and electric grid operation. The city is a complex system in which emerging patterns such as traffic jams, and instabilities or even outages in the electric grid are difficult to predict. The layout of charging stations can alter those patterns in traffic and electric grid operation, with consequences to mobility, air quality, and electric system. The present article presents the concept under the research project SANEVEC. It will build a framework for the optimal determination of the location of EV charging stations in a city based on simulation, which will be able to reproduce the feedback effects between all the variables involved: locations of the stations, traffic patterns, characteristics, and operation of the electricity grid, charging fees and air quality in the city. It will employ artificial intelligence methods to find high-quality station location solutions from the simulations and to predict the air quality in the city.
